g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Volume definitions

Pods can use different volume types, some of which may expose sensitive host resources to containers.

Volume types such as hostPath can provide direct access to the node filesystem and are commonly restricted in security-sensitive environments. Workloads should only be allowed to use volume types required for their operation.

Admission policies can restrict or deny unsafe volume types and validate how volumes are configured before a pod is created." tags="pri-2 level-1" slug="volume-definition"/>
g.data-help:
Volume definitions
Pods can use different volume types, some of which may expose sensitive host resources to containers.
Volume types such as hostPath can provide direct access to the node filesystem and are commonly restricted in security-sensitive environments. Workloads should only be allowed to use volume types required for their operation.
Admission policies can restrict or deny unsafe volume types and validate how volumes are configured before a pod is created.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Host Networking

hostNetwork is technically neither overlay nor underlay networking. The pod shares the node’s network namespace and uses the node’s interfaces and IP addresses directly instead of receiving a normal pod network namespace.

This reduces network isolation, may bypass normal pod-level NetworkPolicy enforcement depending on the CNI, and can expose node-local services, interfaces, and ports to the workload.

Host networking should therefore normally be restricted and only allowed when explicitly required." tags="pri-2 Network level-3" slug="host-network"/>
g.data-help:
Host Networking
hostNetwork is technically neither overlay nor underlay networking. The pod shares the node’s network namespace and uses the node’s interfaces and IP addresses directly instead of receiving a normal pod network namespace.
This reduces network isolation, may bypass normal pod-level NetworkPolicy enforcement depending on the CNI, and can expose node-local services, interfaces, and ports to the workload.
Host networking should therefore normally be restricted and only allowed when explicitly required.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="NetworkPolicy Enforcement

NetworkPolicies are applied to pods, not Kubernetes Services.
A policy selects pods using labels and controls the ingress and/or egress traffic allowed for those pods.

Enforcement happens on the pod network path and ultimately applies to traffic between pod IPs. This means the same policy applies whether traffic reaches a pod through a Service or connects directly to the pod IP.

Services may select the same pods for routing and load balancing, but they are not the enforcement point for NetworkPolicies." tags="info level-2" slug="network-policies"/>
g.data-help:
NetworkPolicy Enforcement
NetworkPolicies are applied to pods, not Kubernetes Services. A policy selects pods using labels and controls the ingress and/or egress traffic allowed for those pods.
Enforcement happens on the pod network path and ultimately applies to traffic between pod IPs. This means the same policy applies whether traffic reaches a pod through a Service or connects directly to the pod IP.
Services may select the same pods for routing and load balancing, but they are not the enforcement point for NetworkPolicies.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Kubelet and API Server Communication

The kubelet is the Kubernetes agent running on each worker node and communicates directly with the Kubernetes API server.

The kubelet acts as a client of the Kubernetes API, registering the node, reporting node and pod status, and watching for pods assigned to its node. Changes are received through API watches, allowing the kubelet to continuously reconcile the desired state with the containers running on the node.

The API server can also connect to the Kubelet API, typically on port 10250, for operations such as container logs, exec, and attach." tags="info level-2 KubernetesCore" slug="kubelet-info"/>
g.data-help:
Kubelet and API Server Communication
The kubelet is the Kubernetes agent running on each worker node and communicates directly with the Kubernetes API server.
The kubelet acts as a client of the Kubernetes API, registering the node, reporting node and pod status, and watching for pods assigned to its node. Changes are received through API watches, allowing the kubelet to continuously reconcile the desired state with the containers running on the node.
The API server can also connect to the Kubelet API, typically on port 10250, for operations such as container logs, exec, and attach.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Kubelet API Access and NodeRestriction

Kubelets authenticate to the Kubernetes API using their node identity and should only be permitted to access resources required for their own node.

The Node authorizer limits what authenticated kubelets can access, while the NodeRestriction admission plugin further restricts which Node and Pod objects a kubelet is allowed to modify.

Together, these controls help prevent a compromised kubelet from modifying other nodes, changing pods assigned to other nodes, or manipulating protected node labels that could influence workload scheduling." tags="pri-2 level-2 KubernetesCore" slug="kubelet-security"/>
g.data-help:
Kubelet API Access and NodeRestriction
Kubelets authenticate to the Kubernetes API using their node identity and should only be permitted to access resources required for their own node.
The Node authorizer limits what authenticated kubelets can access, while the NodeRestriction admission plugin further restricts which Node and Pod objects a kubelet is allowed to modify.
Together, these controls help prevent a compromised kubelet from modifying other nodes, changing pods assigned to other nodes, or manipulating protected node labels that could influence workload scheduling.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Security Logging and Monitoring

Kubernetes security-relevant logs should be collected centrally and forwarded to a remote logging or SIEM platform such as Splunk for monitoring, correlation, alerting, and long-term retention.

Important sources include Kubernetes API audit logs, control-plane component logs, kubelet and container runtime logs, authentication and authorization events, admission controller decisions, CNI/network security logs, and security events generated by runtime detection tools.

Kubernetes Audit Logging is particularly important because it records requests made to the Kubernetes API, including who performed an action, which resource was accessed or modified, and whether the request was allowed or denied.

Logs should be stored outside the cluster or otherwise protected from workloads and compromised nodes to prevent attackers from modifying or deleting security evidence." tags="pri-2 level-1 Logging" slug="remote-logging"/>
g.data-help:
Security Logging and Monitoring
Kubernetes security-relevant logs should be collected centrally and forwarded to a remote logging or SIEM platform such as Splunk for monitoring, correlation, alerting, and long-term retention.
Important sources include Kubernetes API audit logs, control-plane component logs, kubelet and container runtime logs, authentication and authorization events, admission controller decisions, CNI/network security logs, and security events generated by runtime detection tools.
Kubernetes Audit Logging is particularly important because it records requests made to the Kubernetes API, including who performed an action, which resource was accessed or modified, and whether the request was allowed or denied.
Logs should be stored outside the cluster or otherwise protected from workloads and compromised nodes to prevent attackers from modifying or deleting security evidence.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="OCI Container

A container is not a virtual machine, but an isolated Linux process running directly on the worker node’s kernel.

The container runtime creates the process according to the OCI specification and configures its filesystem, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, security controls, environment, and other runtime settings.

Kubernetes typically uses a CRI runtime such as containerd or CRI-O, which in turn uses an OCI runtime such as runc or crun to create and start the container process.

After startup, the workload runs as normal Linux processes isolated and restricted by kernel mechanisms." tags="info level-1" slug="container-oci"/>
g.data-help:
OCI Container
A container is not a virtual machine, but an isolated Linux process running directly on the worker node’s kernel.
The container runtime creates the process according to the OCI specification and configures its filesystem, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, security controls, environment, and other runtime settings.
Kubernetes typically uses a CRI runtime such as containerd or CRI-O, which in turn uses an OCI runtime such as runc or crun to create and start the container process.
After startup, the workload runs as normal Linux processes isolated and restricted by kernel mechanisms.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Scheduler & Controller Manager > API Server

The kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager act as clients of the Kubernetes API and initiate authenticated HTTPS connections to the API server.

Both use list/watch requests to continuously observe cluster state and write changes back through the API. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, while the controller-manager reconciles resources toward their desired state.

All requests are authenticated and authorized by the API server. Neither component accesses etcd directly." tags="info level-2 KubernetesCore" slug="kubernetes-core-to-api"/>
g.data-help:
Scheduler & Controller Manager > API Server
The kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager act as clients of the Kubernetes API and initiate authenticated HTTPS connections to the API server.
Both use list/watch requests to continuously observe cluster state and write changes back through the API. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, while the controller-manager reconciles resources toward their desired state.
All requests are authenticated and authorized by the API server. Neither component accesses etcd directly.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="The kube-controller-manager runs the core controllers responsible for continuously reconciling the desired state stored in Kubernetes with the observed state of the cluster.

It contains multiple independent control loops, including controllers for Nodes, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Jobs, Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, and many other Kubernetes resources.

Controllers continuously list and watch resources through the Kubernetes API.

When the observed state differs from the desired state, they create, update, or delete resources through the API to move the cluster toward the desired state. They do not communicate directly with the scheduler, kubelet, or etcd.

The controller-manager operates using its own authenticated identity and requires broad cluster-wide API permissions because its controllers manage many different resource types.

From a security perspective, the controller-manager is one of the most privileged control-plane components. Compromise of its identity or credentials can provide extensive control over cluster resources, making protection of its credentials, configuration, and host particularly important." tags="info level-2 KubernetesCore" slug="kubernetes-controller-manager"/>
g.data-help:
The kube-controller-manager runs the core controllers responsible for continuously reconciling the desired state stored in Kubernetes with the observed state of the cluster.
It contains multiple independent control loops, including controllers for Nodes, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Jobs, Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, and many other Kubernetes resources.
Controllers continuously list and watch resources through the Kubernetes API.
When the observed state differs from the desired state, they create, update, or delete resources through the API to move the cluster toward the desired state. They do not communicate directly with the scheduler, kubelet, or etcd.
The controller-manager operates using its own authenticated identity and requires broad cluster-wide API permissions because its controllers manage many different resource types.
From a security perspective, the controller-manager is one of the most privileged control-plane components. Compromise of its identity or credentials can provide extensive control over cluster resources, making protection of its credentials, configuration, and host particularly important.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Kube-Scheduler

The kube-scheduler is responsible for selecting which node should run each newly created Pod that has not yet been assigned to a node.

It continuously watches the Kubernetes API for unscheduled Pods and maintains information about Nodes and other resources required to make scheduling decisions. It considers available resources, scheduling constraints, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology, and other scheduling policies.

Once a node has been selected, the scheduler records the decision through the Kubernetes API. It does not communicate directly with the kubelet or etcd.

The scheduler operates using its own authenticated identity and requires cluster-wide read access to several resources, while its write permissions are primarily related to scheduling Pods. Its API access is controlled through Kubernetes authorization, typically RBAC.

From a security perspective, the scheduler is highly trusted because it can influence where workloads execute. However, its API privileges are generally more limited than those of the kube-controller-manager." tags="info level-2 KubernetesCore" slug="kubernetes-scheduler"/>
g.data-help:
Kube-Scheduler
The kube-scheduler is responsible for selecting which node should run each newly created Pod that has not yet been assigned to a node.
It continuously watches the Kubernetes API for unscheduled Pods and maintains information about Nodes and other resources required to make scheduling decisions. It considers available resources, scheduling constraints, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology, and other scheduling policies.
Once a node has been selected, the scheduler records the decision through the Kubernetes API. It does not communicate directly with the kubelet or etcd.
The scheduler operates using its own authenticated identity and requires cluster-wide read access to several resources, while its write permissions are primarily related to scheduling Pods. Its API access is controlled through Kubernetes authorization, typically RBAC.
From a security perspective, the scheduler is highly trusted because it can influence where workloads execute. However, its API privileges are generally more limited than those of the kube-controller-manager.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="font-size: 18px; color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b style="">?</b></font>" help="Kubernetes Resources

Kubernetes resources are API objects that describe the desired or observed
state of the cluster. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets,
Nodes, Roles, and NetworkPolicies.

Resources can be created by users and applications through the Kubernetes API,
or automatically by controllers and other Kubernetes components. Controllers
continuously watch resources and may create, modify, or delete other resources
to reconcile the cluster toward its desired state.

Namespaced resources belong to a specific namespace and are commonly used for
workloads and their configuration. Examples include Pods, Deployments,
Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and Roles.

Cluster-scoped resources exist across the entire cluster and do not belong to
a namespace. Examples include Nodes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles, StorageClasses,
and PersistentVolumes.

All resources are accessed and managed through the Kubernetes API, where
authentication, authorization, admission control, and other security controls
determine who can perform operations on them." tags="info" slug="k8s-resources"/>
g.data-help:
Kubernetes Resources
Kubernetes resources are API objects that describe the desired or observed state of the cluster. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, Nodes, Roles, and NetworkPolicies.
Resources can be created by users and applications through the Kubernetes API, or automatically by controllers and other Kubernetes components. Controllers continuously watch resources and may create, modify, or delete other resources to reconcile the cluster toward its desired state.
Namespaced resources belong to a specific namespace and are commonly used for workloads and their configuration. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and Roles.
Cluster-scoped resources exist across the entire cluster and do not belong to a namespace. Examples include Nodes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles, StorageClasses, and PersistentVolumes.
All resources are accessed and managed through the Kubernetes API, where authentication, authorization, admission control, and other security controls determine who can perform operations on them.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Egress

Egress policies control outbound traffic from pods using label selectors and
destination IPs or CIDRs. These rules help prevent unauthorized external access.

Some CNIs support assigning dedicated egress IPs per namespace or pod,
enabling traceability and firewall integration for outbound traffic control." tags="pri-3 Network level-2" slug="egress"/>
g.data-help:
Egress
Egress policies control outbound traffic from pods using label selectors and destination IPs or CIDRs. These rules help prevent unauthorized external access.
Some CNIs support assigning dedicated egress IPs per namespace or pod, enabling traceability and firewall integration for outbound traffic control.

g.content:
<UserObject label="" help="Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP)

A CNAPP provides centralized security visibility and protection across
Kubernetes, containers, cloud infrastructure, and workloads.

It typically combines vulnerability and image scanning, security posture
management, identity and permission analysis, compliance monitoring, and
runtime threat detection.

A CNAPP helps identify and prioritize risks across multiple security layers
instead of evaluating vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in isolation.

Examples:
Wiz, Sysdig, Prisma Cloud, and Aqua Security.

Open-source building blocks:
Kubescape, Trivy, Falco and NeuVector." tags="pri-2 level-1" slug="cnapp"/>
g.data-help:
Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP)
A CNAPP provides centralized security visibility and protection across Kubernetes, containers, cloud infrastructure, and workloads.
It typically combines vulnerability and image scanning, security posture management, identity and permission analysis, compliance monitoring, and runtime threat detection.
A CNAPP helps identify and prioritize risks across multiple security layers instead of evaluating vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in isolation.
Examples: Wiz, Sysdig, Prisma Cloud, and Aqua Security.
Open-source building blocks: Kubescape, Trivy, Falco and NeuVector.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="NodePort

A NodePort exposes a Service on a static port on every Kubernetes node.

Traffic sent to <NodeIP>:<NodePort> is forwarded by the Kubernetes networking implementation to one of the Service's backend Pods.

NodePort provides basic external reachability, but does not itself provision an external load balancer or public IP." tags="info level-3" slug="node-port"/>
g.data-help:
NodePort
A NodePort exposes a Service on a static port on every Kubernetes node.
Traffic sent to <NodeIP>:<NodePort> is forwarded by the Kubernetes networking implementation to one of the Service's backend Pods.
NodePort provides basic external reachability, but does not itself provision an external load balancer or public IP.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="LoadBalancer

A LoadBalancer Service requests an external load balancer from an integrated cloud provider or load-balancer implementation such as MetalLB.

The load balancer receives an external IP and forwards traffic into the Kubernetes Service, which then distributes traffic to its backend Pods.

A LoadBalancer Service typically builds on the same Service mechanisms as NodePort, although implementations may route traffic differently and can bypass NodePort." tags="info level-3" slug="load-balancer"/>
g.data-help:
LoadBalancer
A LoadBalancer Service requests an external load balancer from an integrated cloud provider or load-balancer implementation such as MetalLB.
The load balancer receives an external IP and forwards traffic into the Kubernetes Service, which then distributes traffic to its backend Pods.
A LoadBalancer Service typically builds on the same Service mechanisms as NodePort, although implementations may route traffic differently and can bypass NodePort.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="NodePort Exposure

By default, Kubernetes reserves ports 30000-32767 for NodePort Services.
A NodePort is normally exposed on eligible network interfaces of every node,
meaning <NodeIP>:<NodePort> can provide an entry point to the Service.

The port range can be changed using the kube-apiserver option:
--service-node-port-range=30000-32767

Which node addresses accept NodePort traffic can be restricted using the
kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses option. This allows NodePort to bind only to
selected node networks, for example an internal network.

Network firewalls should additionally restrict access to the NodePort range
from untrusted networks.

Note: CNI implementations such as Cilium may implement NodePort without
kube-proxy and provide their own configuration for controlling exposure." tags="info level-3" slug="node-port-exposure"/>
g.data-help:
NodePort Exposure
By default, Kubernetes reserves ports 30000-32767 for NodePort Services. A NodePort is normally exposed on eligible network interfaces of every node, meaning <NodeIP>:<NodePort> can provide an entry point to the Service.
The port range can be changed using the kube-apiserver option: --service-node-port-range=30000-32767
Which node addresses accept NodePort traffic can be restricted using the kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses option. This allows NodePort to bind only to selected node networks, for example an internal network.
Network firewalls should additionally restrict access to the NodePort range from untrusted networks.
Note: CNI implementations such as Cilium may implement NodePort without kube-proxy and provide their own configuration for controlling exposure.

g.content:
<UserObject label="<font style="color: rgb(51, 51, 51);"><b>?</b></font>" help="Load Balancer in Front of NodePort

A load balancer provides a controlled external entry point and forwards
traffic to the NodePort on selected Kubernetes nodes.

It provides a stable IP or hostname, distributes traffic between healthy
nodes, and prevents clients from needing direct access to individual nodes.

Firewall rules should restrict NodePort access so that only the load balancer
can reach the exposed ports." tags="info level-3" slug="node-port-exposure-lb"/>
g.data-help:
Load Balancer in Front of NodePort
A load balancer provides a controlled external entry point and forwards traffic to the NodePort on selected Kubernetes nodes.
It provides a stable IP or hostname, distributes traffic between healthy nodes, and prevents clients from needing direct access to individual nodes.
Firewall rules should restrict NodePort access so that only the load balancer can reach the exposed ports.
